lessons.title: Waves in air, fluids and solids
lessons.summary: Compare transverse and longitudinal waves, use the wave equation v = fλ and period T = 1/f, describe how waves are measured in a ripple tank and on a string, and explain how sound, ultrasound and seismic waves are used.
objectives: I can describe the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves and give examples of each.
I can define amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, and use T = 1/f.
I can use the wave equation v = f λ to calculate wave speed, frequency or wavelength.
I can describe how to measure the speed of waves in a ripple tank and on a stretched string.
I can explain what happens when waves meet a boundary and describe uses of ultrasound and seismic waves (Higher).

activities.title: Two types of wave
activities.content:
## Waves transfer energy, not matter

Drop a stone into a pond and ripples spread out, but a leaf floating on the water just bobs up and down: it does not travel with the wave. **Waves transfer energy and information from one place to another without transferring matter.**

### Transverse waves
The **oscillations (vibrations) are at right angles** to the direction the wave travels. Think of a rope shaken up and down: the wave moves along the rope but each bit of rope moves up and down.

Examples: ripples on water, **all electromagnetic waves** (light, radio, X-rays), S-waves in earthquakes, waves on a guitar string.

### Longitudinal waves
The **oscillations are parallel** to the direction the wave travels. A slinky pushed back and forth along its length shows this: sections of coil bunch together (**compressions**) and spread apart (**rarefactions**).

Examples: **sound waves**, ultrasound, P-waves in earthquakes.

```
Transverse:    ~~~~~~~~~~~   particles move ↑↓, wave moves →

Longitudinal:  ||||  |  |  ||||  |  |  ||||   particles move ↔, wave moves →
               comp  rare  comp  rare  comp
```

Longitudinal waves **need a medium** (a material) to travel through; sound cannot cross a vacuum. Electromagnetic waves can travel through empty space.

question.text: Match each description to the correct wave type.
question.hint: Sound needs compressions and rarefactions; light does not.
question.explanation: Sound and P-waves are longitudinal (oscillations parallel to travel). Light and ripples on water are transverse (oscillations perpendicular to travel).

pairs.left: Ripple on the surface of a pond

activities.title: Describing waves
activities.content:
## Wave properties

| Property | Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Amplitude** | $A$ | maximum displacement of a point from its rest (undisturbed) position | m |
| **Wavelength** | $\lambda$ (lambda) | distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest) | m |
| **Frequency** | $f$ | number of complete waves passing a point each second | hertz (Hz) |
| **Period** | $T$ | time for one complete wave to pass a point | s |
| **Wave speed** | $v$ | how fast the energy (the wave) moves through the medium | m/s |

**Amplitude** is measured from the middle line to the crest, **not** from crest to trough.

### Period and frequency
If 5 waves pass each second ($f$ = 5 Hz), each one takes a fifth of a second:

$$T = \frac{1}{f}$$

A frequency of 250 Hz gives a period of $1/250 = 0.004$ s. A period of 0.02 s gives a frequency of $1/0.02 = 50$ Hz.

### The wave equation
In one second, $f$ waves pass by, each of length $\lambda$. The distance travelled per second is the speed:

$$v = f \lambda$$

- $v$ in m/s, $f$ in Hz, $\lambda$ in m

When a wave passes from one medium to another its **speed changes**, its **wavelength changes** but its **frequency stays the same** (the source is still vibrating at the same rate). All sound waves in the same air travel at the same speed regardless of frequency, so high-frequency sounds have shorter wavelengths.

activities.title: Worked example: using the wave equation
activities.content:
**A sound wave in air has a frequency of 440 Hz and a wavelength of 0.75 m. Find its speed.**

$v = f\lambda = 440 \times 0.75 = 330$ m/s

**Radio waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. A station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Find the wavelength.**

100 MHz = 100 × 10⁶ Hz = 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^8}{1.0 \times 10^8} = 3.0$ m

**Water waves in a tank travel at 0.24 m/s with a wavelength of 4 cm. Find the frequency and the period.**

4 cm = 0.04 m

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.24}{0.04} = 6$ Hz

$T = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{6} = 0.17$ s (2 d.p.)

Convert prefixes first: kHz = ×10³, MHz = ×10⁶, cm = ÷100, mm = ÷1000.

question.text: A wave on a rope has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 0.5 m. Calculate the wave speed.
Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. A whistle produces a sound of wavelength 0.17 m. Calculate the period of the sound wave, in seconds.
question.hint: First find the frequency using f = v ÷ λ, then T = 1 ÷ f.

activities.title: Required practical: measuring wave speed
activities.content:
## Water waves in a ripple tank

1. Set up a shallow tray of water with a **motor-driven paddle** (a signal generator sets the frequency) at one end and a lamp above so the wave pattern is projected onto a screen below.
2. **Frequency**: read it from the signal generator, or count the waves passing a point in 10 s and divide by 10.
3. **Wavelength**: place a ruler on the screen and measure the distance across **several** wavelengths (e.g. 10), then divide by 10. This reduces the uncertainty. A **strobe light** flashing at the wave frequency 'freezes' the pattern so it is easier to measure.
4. Calculate **speed = frequency × wavelength**.

An alternative is to time a single wave crest travelling a measured distance across the tank: speed = distance ÷ time.

## Waves on a stretched string

1. Attach a string to a **vibration generator** driven by a signal generator, pass it over a pulley and hang masses on the end to keep it taut.
2. Adjust the frequency until a clear **standing wave** appears with several loops.
3. Measure the length of, say, 4 loops with a metre ruler. Each loop is **half a wavelength**, so wavelength = (length ÷ 4) × 2.
4. Read the frequency from the generator and calculate $v = f\lambda$.

### Measuring the speed of sound in air
Two students stand a measured distance apart (say 100 m or more). One bangs cymbals; the other starts a stopwatch on seeing the clash and stops it on hearing the sound. Speed = distance ÷ time. Repeat and average, because the reaction time is a large fraction of the reading.

question.text: In the ripple tank practical, why is it better to measure the length of ten waves and divide by ten than to measure one wavelength directly?
question.hint: Think about the uncertainty in a ruler reading compared with the size of what you are measuring.
question.explanation: One wavelength may be only a centimetre or two, so a 1 mm ruler uncertainty is a large percentage. Measuring ten wavelengths makes the same absolute uncertainty a much smaller percentage of the reading.

options.text: It reduces the percentage uncertainty in the measurement
Ten waves travel faster than one wave
options.feedback: All waves in the tank travel at the same speed.

options.text: It changes the frequency of the waves
A single wavelength cannot be seen on the screen

activities.title: Waves at a boundary
activities.content:
## What happens when a wave hits a surface?

When a wave reaches the **boundary** between two different materials, three things can happen, often all at once:

- **Reflection**: the wave bounces back. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
- **Absorption**: the wave's energy is taken in by the material (usually transferred to its thermal energy store).
- **Transmission**: the wave passes through into the new material, often changing speed and direction (**refraction**).

Which effect dominates depends on the wavelength of the wave and the material. A mirror reflects visible light strongly; black paper absorbs it; glass transmits it. Thick curtains absorb sound while a hard tiled wall reflects it, which is why bathrooms echo.

## Sound and the ear
Sound waves are longitudinal pressure waves. When they reach the ear they make the **eardrum vibrate** at the same frequency; tiny bones pass the vibration to the inner ear where it is converted to electrical signals. Because this conversion only works over a limited range of frequencies, human hearing is limited to about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz)**. The upper limit falls with age.

Sound travels **faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases**, because the particles are closer together and pass on vibrations more quickly. Typical speeds: air 330 m/s, water 1500 m/s, steel 5000 m/s.

activities.title: Ultrasound and seismic waves (Higher)
activities.content:
## Ultrasound
**Ultrasound** is sound with a frequency **above 20 kHz**, higher than humans can hear. It is useful because it is **partially reflected** at a boundary between two different media.

A pulse is sent out and the **time for the echo to return** is measured. Since speed is known:

$$\text{distance to the boundary} = \frac{\text{speed} \times \text{time}}{2}$$

The **÷2** is essential: the pulse travels there **and back**.

Uses:
- **Medical imaging**, e.g. scanning a foetus: safe because it is non-ionising, unlike X-rays.
- **Industrial testing**: finding cracks inside metal castings without cutting them open.
- **Echo sounding / sonar**: measuring the depth of water or locating shoals of fish.

## Seismic waves
Earthquakes send **seismic waves** through the Earth, detected by **seismometers** around the world.

| | P-waves | S-waves |
|---|---|---|
| Type | longitudinal | transverse |
| Speed | faster (arrive first) | slower |
| Travel through | solids **and** liquids | solids **only** |

S-waves are not detected on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake, creating a **shadow zone**. This tells us the **outer core is liquid**. P-waves are refracted as they pass through layers of different density, and the pattern of their arrival times revealed the size of the core. This is how we know the structure of the Earth's interior without ever drilling into it.

question.text: A ship sends an ultrasound pulse down to the seabed. The echo returns 0.60 s later. Ultrasound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. Calculate the depth of the water.
question.hint: Total distance travelled = speed × time, but the pulse goes down AND back up.

question.text: Which TWO statements about seismic waves are correct?
question.hint: Remember which type can pass through a liquid.
question.explanation: P-waves are longitudinal and travel through both solids and liquids; S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids, which is why they are blocked by the liquid outer core.

options.text: S-waves cannot travel through the liquid outer core
P-waves are longitudinal and can travel through solids and liquids
S-waves travel faster than P-waves
options.feedback: P-waves are the faster ones; they arrive first.

options.text: P-waves are transverse

question.text:
A student uses a ripple tank to measure the speed of water waves. The signal generator is set to 8 Hz. The student measures the distance across 6 wavelengths on the screen as 18 cm.

(a) Calculate the wavelength of the waves in metres. (1 mark)

(b) Calculate the speed of the waves. (2 marks)

(c) Calculate the period of the waves. (1 mark)

(d) Describe two ways the student could improve the accuracy of the wavelength measurement. (2 marks)
question.hint: For (a), 18 cm ÷ 6 gives cm per wave; convert to metres. For (d), think about the strobe light and about measuring more waves.
question.explanation: (a) λ = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 cm = 0.03 m. (b) v = fλ = 8 × 0.03 = 0.24 m/s. (c) T = 1/8 = 0.125 s. (d) Use a strobe light to freeze the pattern; measure across more wavelengths; take a photograph of the screen with a ruler in view; repeat and take a mean.

markScheme.criterion: Use a strobe light / take a photo to freeze the wave pattern
Measure across more wavelengths / repeat and average

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Waves transfer **energy**, not matter. **Transverse**: oscillations at right angles to travel (light, ripples, S-waves). **Longitudinal**: oscillations parallel to travel, with compressions and rarefactions (sound, P-waves).
- **Amplitude** (rest to crest), **wavelength** (crest to crest), **frequency** (waves per second, Hz), **period** $T = 1/f$.
- **Wave equation**: $v = f\lambda$. Frequency is fixed by the source; speed and wavelength change when the medium changes.
- Measure wave speed in a **ripple tank** (frequency from generator, wavelength across several waves) or on a **string** (each loop = half a wavelength).
- At a boundary waves are **reflected, absorbed or transmitted**. Humans hear **20 Hz – 20 kHz**.
- (Higher) **Ultrasound** echoes: distance = speed × time ÷ 2. **P-waves** pass through liquids, **S-waves** do not, proving the outer core is liquid.

practiceQuestions.text: In a longitudinal wave, the oscillations are:
practiceQuestions.hint: Think of a slinky being pushed and pulled along its length.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In a longitudinal wave the particles oscillate parallel to (along) the direction of energy transfer.

options.text: parallel to the direction the wave travels
at right angles to the direction the wave travels
in circles
always vertical

metadata.blanksText: The ___ of a wave is the number of waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz. The ___ is the distance from one crest to the next crest.

practiceQuestions.hint: One is measured in Hz, the other in metres.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Frequency is waves per second; wavelength is the crest-to-crest distance.

practiceQuestions.text: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate its period.
Water waves travel at 1.5 m/s with a wavelength of 0.3 m. Calculate their frequency.
A radio wave has a frequency of 200 kHz and travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
practiceQuestions.hint: Convert kHz to Hz (× 1000) first, then λ = v ÷ f.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: when a sound wave passes from air into water its frequency stays the same but its wavelength changes.
practiceQuestions.hint: The source vibrates at a fixed rate, but the speed of sound is different in water.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Frequency is set by the source. Sound travels faster in water, so with the same frequency the wavelength must be longer (v = fλ).

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: A standing wave on a string has 5 loops along a length of 1.25 m. Calculate the wavelength.
practiceQuestions.hint: Each loop is half a wavelength. Find the length of one loop, then double it.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of the following are true about human hearing?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the frequency range and how the ear detects sound.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. Ultrasound is above the hearing range, and hearing range decreases with age rather than increasing.

options.text: The normal range of hearing is about 20 Hz to 20 kHz
Sound waves cause the eardrum to vibrate
Humans can hear ultrasound
The upper limit of hearing increases as people get older

practiceQuestions.text: An ultrasound scanner sends a pulse into a metal block. An echo from a crack inside the block returns after 0.00004 s. The speed of ultrasound in the metal is 5000 m/s. Calculate the depth of the crack below the surface in metres.
practiceQuestions.hint: Distance there and back = speed × time. Halve it for the depth.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how the study of seismic waves provides evidence that the Earth has a liquid outer core.
practiceQuestions.hint: Which type of wave cannot travel through a liquid, and what do seismometers on the far side of the Earth detect?
practiceQuestions.explanation: S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids. Seismometers on the opposite side of the Earth from an earthquake do not detect S-waves (a shadow zone), so part of the Earth's interior must be liquid. P-waves do pass through but are refracted, confirming the size of the core.

markScheme.criterion: S-waves are not detected on the opposite side of the Earth / there is a shadow zone
P-waves pass through / are refracted by the core

practiceQuestions.text:
A student measures the speed of sound by standing 240 m from a wall and clapping. She hears the echo 1.5 s after clapping.

(a) Calculate the speed of sound from her results. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why her value is likely to be inaccurate and suggest how she could improve the experiment. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is 480 m.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Distance = 2 × 240 = 480 m. Speed = 480 ÷ 1.5 = 320 m/s. (b) Her reaction time when starting and stopping the stopwatch is a large fraction of 1.5 s. She could clap repeatedly in time with the echoes and time many echoes, or use a data logger with a microphone, or repeat and take a mean.

markScheme.criterion: Reaction time is significant compared with the measured time
Improvement: time many echoes / use a microphone and data logger / repeat and average

practiceQuestions.text: Match each wave example to the correct wave type.
practiceQuestions.hint: In a longitudinal wave the particles move backwards and forwards along the same line the wave travels along.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ultrasound is a sound wave, so it is longitudinal, and a slinky pushed and pulled along its length carries compressions and rarefactions, which is also longitudinal. Seismic S-waves and microwaves both have oscillations at right angles to the direction of travel, so they are transverse.

pairs.left: Ultrasound pulse travelling through the body
Pulse along a slinky that is pushed and pulled along its length
Microwave sent from a phone mast

practiceQuestions.text: A tuning fork vibrates at 256 Hz and produces sound waves in air with a wavelength of 1.25 m. Calculate the speed of sound in the air.
practiceQuestions.hint: Use $v = f\lambda$ and give a unit with your answer.

practiceQuestions.text: Waves on a lake travel at 3.0 m/s and have a wavelength of 1.2 m. Calculate the period of the waves, in seconds.
practiceQuestions.hint: Rearrange $v = f\lambda$ to find the frequency first, then use $T = 1 \div f$.

practiceQuestions.text: A student wants to find the frequency of the waves in a ripple tank. Instead of timing how long one wave takes to pass a mark on the screen, she counts how many waves pass the mark in 20 s. Why is her method better?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the reaction time on a stopwatch with the time being measured in each case.
practiceQuestions.explanation: One wave passes the mark in a fraction of a second, so the student's reaction time (a few tenths of a second) would be a large fraction of the reading. Counting waves over 20 s makes the same reaction-time error a much smaller percentage of the measurement.

options.text: The reaction-time error becomes a much smaller percentage of the measured time
Counting the waves slows them down so they are easier to time
options.feedback: Observing the waves has no effect on their speed.

options.text: The frequency of the waves increases over 20 s
options.feedback: The signal generator keeps the frequency constant.

options.text: It is impossible to see a single wave on the screen

practiceQuestions.text: A bat emits an ultrasound click and detects the echo from a cave wall 0.050 s later. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m/s. Calculate the distance between the bat and the wall.
practiceQuestions.hint: The click travels to the wall and back again, so the distance from speed × time is twice the distance you want.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Total distance travelled $= 340 \times 0.050 = 17$ m. This is there and back, so distance to the wall $= 17 \div 2 = 8.5$ m.

practiceQuestions.text: After an earthquake, seismometers around the world record the waves that arrive. Which TWO statements correctly describe what these records show?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what happens to each type of wave when it reaches a liquid, and how P-waves behave at boundaries between layers.
practiceQuestions.explanation: S-waves are transverse and cannot pass through a liquid, so they are not detected on the far side of the Earth; this shows part of the core is liquid. P-waves are refracted (change speed and direction) as they cross boundaries between layers of different density, which produces shadow zones and tells us about the size of the core. S-waves do not pass through the liquid outer core at all, and P-waves travel through solids as well as liquids.

options.text: S-waves are not detected on the opposite side of the Earth, which shows that part of the core is liquid
P-waves change speed and direction as they pass through layers of different density
S-waves pass through the liquid outer core but are slowed down
options.feedback: S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through a liquid at all.

options.text: P-waves cannot travel through solid rock
options.feedback: P-waves are longitudinal and travel through both solids and liquids.

practiceQuestions.text:
A student investigates water waves in a ripple tank. The signal generator driving the paddle is set to 5 Hz. The student measures the distance across 10 wavelengths on the screen as 25 cm.

(a) Calculate the wavelength of the waves in metres. (1 mark)

(b) Calculate the speed of the waves. (2 marks)

(c) Calculate the period of the waves. (1 mark)

(d) Suggest two ways the student could make the wavelength measurement more reliable. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), divide 25 cm by 10 and convert to metres. For (d), think about freezing the moving pattern and about how many waves are measured.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) $\lambda = 25 \div 10 = 2.5$ cm $= 0.025$ m. (b) $v = f\lambda = 5 \times 0.025 = 0.125$ m/s. (c) $T = 1 \div 5 = 0.2$ s. (d) Use a strobe light or take a photograph so the pattern appears still; measure across an even larger number of wavelengths; repeat the measurement and take a mean.

markScheme.criterion: Use a strobe light / photograph to freeze the pattern
Measure across more wavelengths / repeat and take a mean
